title: Review: Electrical power and energy; EMF and internal resistance; Capacitor charging and discharging; Magnetic fields and field patterns
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Physics 2 (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: MG01-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; EL08-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; EL10-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; MG01-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL05-1#N.3, EL08-1#N.5b, EL10-1#N.8, MG01-1#N.3, EL05-1#N.5, EL08-1#N.10, EL10-1#N.9b, MG01-1#N.5, EL05-1#N.11b, EL08-1#N.3, MG01-1#N.7. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Compass needle
items.clue: Pointer whose north end shows which way the pattern runs at that place.

items.label: Internal resistance
items.clue: Property r of a real cell, treated as sitting in series with an ideal cell.

items.label: Time constant
items.clue: Symbol τ: after one, 37% of a discharging capacitor's starting charge is left.

items.label: Magnetic field
items.clue: Region produced by moving charges that pushes on currents and on iron or steel.

questions.stem: The potential difference across an ohmic resistor is increased so that the current in the resistor becomes three times as large. What is the ratio of the new power dissipated in the resistor, P₂, to the original power, P₁?
questions.explanation: The resistor is ohmic, so R is unchanged. P = I²R: tripling I multiplies P by 3² = 9.

questions.stem: A battery of emf ε and internal resistance r is connected to an external resistor of resistance R. What is the potential difference across the terminals of the battery?

An uncharged capacitor is charged through a 3.0 kΩ resistor by an ideal battery of emf 9.0 V, all connected in series. What is the current in the resistor at the instant when the potential difference across the capacitor is 6.0 V?
Point C is at the centre of a bar magnet, inside it. Point D is just outside the magnet, beside its centre. How does the magnitude of the magnetic field at C compare with that at D?

options.text: Greater at D, as field lines end at the poles and none is inside
Zero at both points, since the middle of a magnet is not magnetic
The same at both, as the magnet's field has one strength everywhere
Greater at C, as the closed field lines are crowded inside the magnet

questions.stem: A steady current of 0.25 A flows in a 24 Ω resistor for 2.0 minutes. How much energy is dissipated in the resistor?
questions.explanation: Power = I²R = 0.25² × 24 = 1.5 W. Energy = power × time = 1.5 W × 120 s = 180 J.

questions.stem: A battery of internal resistance r is connected to an external resistor whose resistance equals r. The external resistor is then replaced by one of resistance 2r. How does the potential difference across the terminals of the battery change?

options.text: It stays equal to its first value.
It rises to 2 times its first value.
It falls to 2/3 of its first value.
It increases to 4/3 of its first value.

questions.stem: A 2.0 μF capacitor is charged to a potential difference of 6.0 V. At t = 0 it is connected across a 1.0 MΩ resistor and begins to discharge. What is the magnitude of the charge on each plate of the capacitor at t = 2.0 s?
A long, straight, vertical wire carries a steady current upwards. Point P is 5.0 cm due east of the wire, level with it. What is the direction of the magnetic field of the wire at P?

options.text: Due south, at a tangent to a circle around the wire
Due east, directly away from the wire along a radius
Due north, at a tangent to a circle centred on the wire
Vertically upwards, parallel to the direction of the current

questions.explanation: Right thumb up, along the current: the fingers curl around the wire, and on its east side they point due north. The field is a tangent to a circle centred on the wire.

questions.stem: Two identical heating coils, each of resistance R, are connected to the same ideal battery: first in series, then in parallel. What is the total power in parallel divided by the total power in series?
questions.explanation: Series: R_eq = 2R, so P = ΔV²/2R. Parallel: R_eq = R/2, so P = 2ΔV²/R. Ratio: (2ΔV²/R) ÷ (ΔV²/2R) = 4.

questions.stem: A battery with an internal resistance of 0.50 Ω drives a current of 0.60 A through a lamp, and an ideal voltmeter across the battery's terminals reads 4.2 V. The lamp is then disconnected, so that only the voltmeter remains connected across the battery. What does the voltmeter now read?
questions.explanation: emf = terminal potential difference + Ir = 4.2 + 0.60 × 0.50 = 4.5 V. With no current, the voltmeter reads the emf.

questions.stem: You look at the left end of a long solenoid. Seen from there, the current in its turns flows clockwise. Which end of the solenoid is its north end?

options.text: The left end, the one you are looking at
The right end, the far end from you
Neither: inside, the field is uniform, so there are no poles
It depends on the size of the current in the turns

questions.explanation: Fingers clockwise as seen from the left, so the thumb points to the right. Inside, the field runs left to right and leaves through the right end. Field lines leave a north end, so that end is N.
